newsitem.title: JAPAN: SOCCER-JAPAN'S J-LEAGUE WORRIED ABOUT DROP IN SUPPORT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JAPAN'S J-LEAGUE WORRIED ABOUT DROP IN SUPPORT.

text.p: Japanese soccer officials are worried for the future of the sport as fans continue to drift away from the professional J-League.
Figures released on Monday show the average attendance for matches in the first stage of this season, which ended last week, fell to 10,611 from 13,353 last year.
"We are a bit worried about the future of J-League," J-League spokesman Hiroshi Kagayama admitted to Reuters.
The second stage of the season starts on July 30 but many of Japan's stars will be absent because of the two-month schedule of the Asia Cup Finals between September and November.
When the J-League was launched in 1993, professional football was booming in Japan with capacity crowds and millions watching on television. The average crowd per game in 1993 was 17,976.
But dwindling crowds and a lack of interest from television stations were the inevitable downside of a freak boom which accompanied the J-league's launch, officials said.
At the start of this year's season in March, officials set their overall target attendance at five million -- less than the six million they easily reached in 1995.
Kagayama said the number of women fans in their 20s and 30s was declining but the number of people attending regularly was on the rise.
The top teams continue to draw large crowds, with first stage-winner Kashima Antlers managing an average of 17,800 spectators per match.
While the J-League has drawn praise for its efforts to promote local communities, the league has also come under criticism for its numerous tournaments and complex schedules.
"We have to think about ways to attract more people," Kagayama said.

League officials said they hoped the 2002 World Cup, to be co-hosted by Japan and South Korea, would help to boost the popularity of soccer in Japan, where the most popular spectator sport is baseball.
"We hope that Japan's co-hosting of the 2002 World Cup with South Korea would be a lever to boost the number of fans," Kagayama said.
As proof that soccer in Japan can still ignite the public's interest, a Tokyo match in May between the two 2002 host countries drew a capacity crowd of nearly 60,000.
